entries.tutorialSubtitle: A reversing twill that produces a V-pattern cloth on a four-shaft floor loom
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Herringbone twill reverses direction every eight to sixteen threads to produce a chevron pattern across the cloth. The structure uses the same threading and tie-up as a standard 2/2 twill but with the threading sequence mirrored at regular intervals. The resulting cloth has the diagonal texture of twill but with a woven-in pattern that does not require colour change.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: A textured cell-pattern fabric on a four-shaft floor loom using a simple tie-up and treadling
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Honeycomb weave produces a fabric with raised hexagonal cells in the cloth surface: the cells trap air and give the cloth excellent insulation. The structure uses only two treadles in alternation on a four-shaft loom and is easier to treadle than twill or overshot. This entry covers a standard cotton honeycomb set up for a sampler or tea towel.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: Preparing raw or washed fleece into fluffy rolags for woollen spinning using hand cards
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Hand carders are a pair of paddle-shaped tools with fine wire teeth used to open, align, and blend fleece fibres before spinning. The process produces a rolag: a loose cylindrical roll of prepared fibre ready for the woollen draw on a wheel or spindle. Hand cards are more portable and slower than a drum carder but give the spinner more control over small quantities and fibre blends.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: A wool-hooked rug with a bold geometric design on hessian backing, using a traditional rug hook
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Rug hooking pulls loops of cut wool strips through a hessian or linen backing using a blunt hook. A geometric design (squares, triangles, or chevrons) is the most manageable for a first rug because the colour boundaries are straight lines and the fill areas are large. A finished rug approximately 40 x 60 cm requires 200-300 g of wool strips.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: Merino roving felted into lightweight silk organza to produce a sheer, textured cloth
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Nuno felt a 60 x 60 cm scarf or panel by laying fine merino roving directly onto silk organza and wet-felting the two together. As the merino shrinks and locks into the open weave of the organza, the silk gathers and scrunches into a pleated, textured surface. The finished cloth is lightweight, drapy, and machine-hand-washable at 30 degrees.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: Using a second dye bath to deepen, shift, or correct the colour of previously dyed fibre
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Overdyeing passes already-dyed fibre through a second dye bath to mix the two colours. The result depends on the starting colour and the overdye: yellow over blue gives green, red over yellow gives orange. Overdyeing is also useful for correcting colours that are too pale, too pink, or not quite the intended shade.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: A high-hydration French loaf with an open crumb and thick crust, made from a very wet dough.
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Pain rustique is a French country loaf built from a slack, high-hydration dough. The wetness produces a wide, irregular crumb with large pockets and a crust that shatters when you cut it. The dough is too sticky to knead by hand in the usual sense; instead, a series of short stretch-and-fold sequences builds the gluten over two hours. One loaf takes about four hours from mixing to the oven.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: Apulian white bread with an open crumb and crisp crust
entries.tutorialExcerpt: A large, round Apulian loaf with a thick, crackly crust and an open, moist crumb. The dough is wetter than a standard white loaf and is coaxed rather than kneaded, relying on stretch-and-fold passes during the bulk rise to build strength without degassing. Baked in a covered dutch oven for the first part of cooking, which traps steam and gives the crust its characteristic shattering quality.

entries.tutorialSubtitle: Italian yeasted fried dough balls dusted with icing sugar
entries.tutorialExcerpt: Simple Italian street food: soft, yeasted dough made into small balls or ring shapes and deep-fried until puffed and golden, then dusted generously with icing sugar. The dough is wet and loose, almost a batter, dropped by the spoonful directly into the oil. The result is light, irregular dough balls with a yeasty, slightly crisp exterior and a tender, airy interior. Made for the feast of San Giuseppe (19 March).
